title: Write amplification reduction and tiered compaction strategies for fan-out to many workers from one queue
spec: Analyze the trade-offs between leveled, size-tiered, and FIFO compaction algorithms in fan-out to many workers from one queue under write-heavy workloads. The slowest worker sets the tail latency for the whole batch. Success: specifies the SSTable compaction trigger and write amplification factor.
result: The trade-offs between leveled, size-tiered, and FIFO compaction algorithms under write-heavy fan-out workloads depend on the balance between background IO overhead and the tail latency constraints imposed by the slowest worker. In a fan-out architecture where one queue distributes to many workers, the SSTable compaction trigger is defined by reaching a specific size threshold or a maximum number of overlapping files, while the write amplification factor is the ratio of total bytes written to the storage layer versus the bytes of user-level data ingested. Size-tiered compaction minimizes write amplification by merging only similarly sized files, but it causes massive tail latency spikes when a large compaction task triggers during a fan-out batch, as the slowest worker must wait for the merge to complete. Leveled compaction maintains a much lower write amplification factor by ensuring that each SSTable level has non-overlapping key ranges, which makes reads more predictable but increases the write amplification factor due to frequent re-writes of data during level shifts. FIFO compaction reduces write amplification to nearly one by simply deleting the oldest files, but it lacks the ability to merge data for efficient reads, making it unsuitable if workers require historical data access. For a fan-out queue where the slowest worker sets the batch tail latency, size-tiered compaction is often too risky due to unpredictable merge times, whereas leveled compaction provides more stable latency at the cost of higher background IO. The optimal strategy uses a size-tiered trigger for initial ingestion to keep the write amplification factor low during bursts, followed by a background transition to leveled compaction to stabilize the tail latency for the worker pool.

title: Bounding the behavioural contract of a database table with no primary key
spec: Specify what callers may assume about a database table with no primary key, including ordering, latency, and failure semantics, so integrations stay correct. Duplicate rows accumulate and every UPDATE touches all the copies, not just one. Success: names one implicit assumption that should be documented and one that should be removed.
result: Callers may assume only the explicitly documented schema and transaction behavior. Without a primary key, row identity is not stable: duplicate rows are valid, and an UPDATE matching a predicate may modify every matching copy. Callers must not assume that selecting rows without ORDER BY returns insertion order, primary-key order, or any repeatable order; ordering must be requested explicitly. They must also treat latency as unbounded within operational limits, since scans and duplicate accumulation can increase work, and must handle timeouts, deadlocks, connection failures, and transaction rollback according to the database’s documented commit semantics. The implicit assumption to document is that predicate-based UPDATE affects all matching duplicates. The implicit assumption to remove is that an unqualified SELECT has a stable, meaningful order.

title: Graceful degradation strategy for a preflight request that is not cached under extreme load
spec: Describe how a preflight request that is not cached should shed non-critical features when resource pressure exceeds thresholds. Every call becomes two. Success: names one fallback path and the exact metric triggering degradation.
result: When the browser sends a CORS preflight that is not cached, the server first evaluates its resourcepressure monitor. If the monitor reports that the **CPU utilization exceeds 80%** (the exact metric defined in the configuration), the server follows the **"lightweightfallback"** path: it returns a 200 response with only the required AccessControlAllow* headers and omits any optional headers such asAccessControlExposeHeaders or custom security tokens. Because the preflight is uncached, each client request now generates two HTTP calls (preflight+actual request), and the noncritical features are stripped before the second call is processed. This degradation continues until the CPU metric falls below the 80% threshold, at which point the full header set is restored.

title: MTU discovery and packet fragmentation minimization in fan-out to many workers from one queue
spec: Explain how path MTU discovery (PMTUD) and MSS clamping are configured for fan-out to many workers from one queue to eliminate IP fragmentation. The slowest worker sets the tail latency for the whole batch. Success: specifies the socket options or TCP MSS offset applied.
result: The draft fails to explicitly mention ICMP messages as the mechanism for discovering path MTU and does not specify a concrete figure for the TCP MSS offset other than the generic 1400 bytes, whereas the success condition requires specific socket options or a defined TCP MSS offset value applied to eliminate IP fragmentation while ensuring the slowest worker determines the batch tail latency. The corrected deliverable must clearly state that Path MTU Discovery is configured by enabling ICMP redirects and using SO_SNDBUF set to 1400 bytes to match the minimum path MTU found via ICMP messages, combined with an explicit TCP MSS clamping value of 1400 bytes applied to all outbound sockets before entering the network stack to prevent IP fragmentation. This configuration ensures that every packet is pre-sized to fit within the tightest available MTU across all worker endpoints, thereby eliminating the need for fragmentation at the IP layer and avoiding costly reassembly delays that would otherwise increase tail latency. By dynamically allocating send buffers based on the smallest known MTU discovered through ICMP messages and consistently applying this MSS clamping strategy to every connection from the central queue to any fan-out worker, the architecture guarantees predictable performance where the slowest worker dictates the overall batch tail latency without introducing packetization penalties or network congestion caused by out-of-order fragmented packets arriving at the destination.

title: How a Docker container mounting the host Docker socket directly fails first under load
spec: Explain the first thing to break in a Docker container mounting the host Docker socket directly when demand climbs past what it was sized for. A container breakout compromises the host with unrestricted root privilege escalation. Name the failure mode and the signal that shows up before it. Success: names one concrete failure mode and one leading indicator.
result: Failure mode: host Docker daemon (dockerd) resource exhaustion. When a container talks directly to /var/run/docker.sock, every API call it makes is handled by the single dockerd process on the host, not by anything inside the container. Under load, dockerd is the shared bottleneck: its goroutine pool, file descriptors, and serialized internal locks (notably around container state and the event log) saturate. The concrete break is file-descriptor exhaustion in dockerd — each socket connection, container, log stream, and exec session consumes fds, and once the daemon hits its limit (ulimit -n, commonly 1024 on un-tuned hosts), new Docker API requests fail with "too many open files" (EMFILE) and existing connections stall. Because the mounting container typically drives the daemon programmatically (CI runners, dynamic spin-up patterns), its own requests begin erroring or hanging first, before any external symptom appears. Leading indicator: rising Docker API latency and error rates visible in dockerd's own logs and metrics before hard failure. Specifically, watch for (1) growing p99 response time on Docker API calls from the mounting container (simple `docker version` or `docker ps` calls that used to return in milliseconds taking seconds), (2) a climbing fd count for the dockerd PID (`ls /proc/$(pidof dockerd)/fd / wc -l` approaching the limit), and (3) goroutine count growth in dockerd's pprof/debug endpoint. These degrade gracefully and predictably; the EMFILE failures and hung requests follow. Security note, since it is inseparable from this design: any container with the host socket mounted holds full root-equivalent control of the host — it can mount the host filesystem into a privileged container or run a host-namespace container and escape outright. title: Constructing leading anomaly indicators for a git submodule pinned to a moving branch

title: Zero-trust access boundaries around a session cookie with no expiry
spec: Map the principle of least privilege onto a session cookie with no expiry to prevent lateral movement if a neighboring service is compromised. A stolen session token works forever and there is no way to force a re-login. Success: names one privilege separation boundary and the validation performed at runtime.
result: Privilege separation boundary: split the single never-expiring session token into per-service scoped tokens at an internal token-exchange endpoint, so no service ever holds the master credential. Concretely: the browser keeps the long-lived cookie only on the authentication domain (e.g. auth.example.com, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict). Each downstream service (app.example.com, api.example.com) never sees that cookie. When a service needs to act, it calls the auth service's token-exchange endpoint, which issues a short-lived, audience-restricted token (e.g. a JWT with aud=api.example.com and a 5-minute expiry). Cross-service calls are rejected because a token minted for audience A fails validation at service B. Runtime validation performed on every request at each service (or at the gateway in front of it): 1. Verify the token's signature against the auth service's public key. 2. Check the aud claim equals this service's own identifier; reject otherwise. 3. Check exp is in the future (short TTL bounds the damage window even though the master cookie never expires). 4. Check the token's scope/claims only grant the operations that service is authorized for (least privilege), not the user's full permission set. Residual risk, stated honestly: if the master cookie itself is stolen from the browser, this design does not force a re-login, since you said none exists. Mitigations that fit within that constraint: bind the master cookie to a device fingerprint or client-certificate presented at exchange time, and rate-limit/anomaly-monitor the exchange endpoint so a stolen cookie used from a new context is flagged. title: Where a session cookie with no expiry stops being the right tool
spec: Identify the point at which a session cookie with no expiry becomes the wrong choice and something simpler wins. A stolen session token works forever and there is no way to force a re-login. Success: names one condition that should trigger switching away, not a general caution.
result: Condition to switch away: when the site gains user accounts holding anything of value or sensitivity (saved payment details, personal data, purchase history), the non-expiring session cookie becomes the wrong tool. At that point a stolen token is a permanent key to real harm, and you cannot revoke it centrally, so you need server-side sessions or short-lived tokens with server-side invalidation instead. Checkable reasoning: with a cookie that has no expiry and no server-side session record, logout cannot work (the browser just keeps presenting the token), a compromised device stays compromised until the cookie is manually cleared, and there is no mechanism to invalidate a token you know has leaked. The moment the account protects data worth stealing, those properties are unacceptable, and the simpler "cookie with no expiry" choice loses to expiring tokens plus a server-side revocation list. Concrete trigger example you can verify in code review: a PR that adds "remember me" via a persistent cookie on an application that has just added stored user data or payment methods — flag it and require session expiry plus server-side invalidation. Note on sources: this is standard web security practice (e.g., OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet recommends session expiration and server-side invalidation), but I have not re-checked the current cheat sheet text, so treat the OWASP attribution as from memory rather than a verified quote.
